For reviewers · FARII consortium · updated 1 October 2026

Which numbers are current, and where each comes from.

This site records several iterations, built on different simulated worlds. Every number below says which world it comes from, what it is scored against and how future pumping is handled. No real water-level measurement has been used anywhere.

Current numbers: the state-space model (Stage 2)

Test year August 2025 – July 2026, a forecast every Sunday for 579 wells. The method and the expected results were fixed and fingerprinted before any run, and the test year was scored once.

Model, dataset A0.52 m0.61 m0.74 m

Faulty level sensors found: 88 % (A), 80 % (B). The 80 % bands under-cover in A and B (30–67 %). Slow ridge and low-yield wells read about 1 m too deep. Full results.

Why the two forecasters report different numbers

They run on different simulated cities, so both sets of numbers can be true at once. Neither has been checked on real wells.

ML forecaster (team's response)State-space model (Stage 2)
Simulated cityThe team's typed + paved five-year twinOur Phase 2 city (A, B), plus harder worlds C–E
12-week error, against assuming no change0.84 m against 1.01 m0.74 m against 1.48 m (A); 1.52 m against 3.57 m (D, Bengaluru-calibrated rain)
Value of rainRain features worth 0.00 at horizons of days; no claim at weeksRemoves 38 % of the 12-week error in A, about a third in D; little a week ahead
Neighbouring wellsNo neighbour termA simple distance-based term: neighbours' pumping within 1.5 km. Not the crack network on Wells affect each other, which is a separate exploration.
GeologyNone in the twinHidden terrain types shape the city; the model sees them only through imperfect public-quality maps

How much rain helps is a property of the simulated city as much as of the model. It depends on how much recharge comes from rain rather than steady leakage, how long rain takes to arrive, and how much the level moves at all. Where assuming no change is only about 1 m off at 12 weeks, there is little movement left for rain to explain. In our city, rain reaches the water table weeks to months late, so rain that has already fallen predicts the coming weeks. Real records will show which city is closer to Bengaluru.

Harder worlds: well loss and a Bengaluru-calibrated rain response

Two review points were tested on new simulated cities. The model's settings were unchanged.

Model's lead over it at 12 weeks (skill)+0.50+0.51+0.57+0.59
Wells never fitted, 12 weeks ahead1.01 m1.09 m2.48 m2.45 m
Faulty level sensors found88 %79 %100 %81 %
"80 % likely" range held, 12 weeks ahead63 %64 %79 %79 %
Error removed by rain data, 12 weeks ahead38 %32 %33 %30 %

Same model settings in every world. A uses Phase 2 dataset A. C adds a non-linear well loss (drawdown growing with the square of the pumping rate) that the model does not contain. D recalibrates the simulator's rain response to measured Bengaluru levels. E combines C and D.

Non-linear well loss: the model holds up

Accuracy is unchanged even though the model has no such term. The cost falls on the sensor check, which relies on pump power tracking depth: it finds 79 % of faulty sensors instead of 88 %.

Bengaluru-like rain: much harder, still well ahead

Calibrated to 154 Bengaluru borewells (Sekhar et al. 2018), levels swing about 2.4 times as much. Holding the reading flat is then 3.6 m off at 12 weeks; the model is 1.5 m off. Its ranges become honest (79 %), and rain data still removes about a third of the 12-week error.

A weakness found and fixed

In world E, two near-surface wells had a sensor offset that made their readings look above ground. The first version dropped those readings as impossible and drifted hundreds of metres. Three guards were added after scoring (v1.1): above-ground readings are kept as possible offsets, no well is fitted on too little data, and estimates stay within 0–300 m. A is unchanged; E's 12-week error fell from 2.41 m to 1.46 m.

How the simulator was calibrated to Bengaluru
MeasureMeasured (Sekhar et al. 2018)Simulator beforeAfter calibration
Rise after the extreme rain, July → September 201713.3 m2.5 m9.4 m
Drought year 20165.4 m deeper2.8 m deeper3.6 m deeper
Share of rain that recharges (paper's method)13.5 %5.7 %17.8 %
Shallowest month in 2016AugustJanuaryAugust
Depth to water, mean25.7 m29.0 m20.6 m

Targets and tolerances were written down before any calibration run. Calibration ran on 2015–2017 rain scaled to the city's rain gauges. It needed faster recharge and a smaller specific yield (close to the paper's 0.005); the actual recharge is 11.5 % of rain. The rise and the drought fall are still weaker than measured, though within the pre-set bands.

Read every figure as an upper bound
  • Most simulated wells obey the model's own core equations: a store that drains toward a base level, deepened by pumping, raised by delayed recharge. World C adds a non-linear well loss the model does not contain.
  • How much rain helps a forecast depends on how a twin's recharge is built. In our Bengaluru-calibrated world, rain data removes about a third of the 12-week error. A twin with mostly constant leakage will show far less.
  • The simulated city puts valleys shallower than ridges. Measurements in Bengaluru (Sekhar et al. 2018) find the opposite.
What real data would settle
  • Real water levels, ideally with a 48-hour pump-off rest once a month on slow wells.
  • Well locations, or the terrain values the data holder computes for each well.
  • The per-well monthly Bengaluru series behind Sekhar et al. (2018), for a well-by-well calibration.
Borewell Forecast is a proof of concept for forecasting groundwater levels in Bengaluru borewells. Results are labelled by where the data came from: vendor export (15 days, July 2026, in the vendor's real format but with demonstration water-level values), synthetic test system (450 simulated wells with a known answer) or digital twin (physics-based simulations of the 579 wells: one year in iteration 1, five years in later iterations and in Stage 2). No real water-level measurement has been used yet, and nothing here is yet a validated field forecast. Built by the FARII consortium.
